children: U.S. stocks fell for the fourth straight session and Treasury yields hit multiyear highs as U.S. oil prices topped the $100-per-barrel level, while August inflation data revealed the toll energy costs are taking on commercial users.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 316.56 points, or 0.60%, to 52064.10. The S&P 500 lost 44.66 points, or 0.58%, to 7591.70 and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite declined 171.62 points, or 0.65%, to 26081.72.

Oil futures rose $6.43, or 6.7% to $102.48 a barrel, the highest settlement since May 19. This was oil's eighth straight gain, the longest winning streak in three years. The gains reflect a growing sense that the U.S. and Iran are hunkering down for a war of attrition. The U.S. is squeezing Iran's economy while the government in Tehran is flexing its influence on global energy markets.

The producer price index rose 0.4% in August from the July rate, and was up 5.4% from a year earlier due to the recent spike in oil prices. The knock-on effect on diesel prices was particularly marked, economists said.

"September's surge in energy prices will likely tip the balance towards a hike when the Fed meets next week," Fifth Third Commercial Bank's chief U.S. economist Bill Adams said in e-mailed commentary.

The yield on the 30-year bond rose 0.075 percentage point to 5.360%, the highest close since June 2004. The yield on the 10-year Treasury added 0.104 percentage point to 4.943% for its biggest gain since May and its highest close since October 2023. The yield on the policy-sensitive two-year Treasury rose 0.122 percentage point to 4.548%, the largest increase since March and the highest close in more than two years.
The U.S. dollar rose after the wholesale inflation data.

Dollar-sensitive gold futures shed $51.50, or 1.2%, to $4364.50 a troy ounce. Copper futures slid 33.65 cents, or 4.95%, to $6.4670 a pound, falling from record highs for its biggest one-day decline in more than a year. A White House plan to broaden tariffs on imports of refined copper has stalled because of the ramifications for U.S. manufacturers, Reuters reported.

In recent weeks, the prices of commodities such as diesel and copper have hit all-time highs, while grains have reached their highest prices since the start of the war with Iran. That has raised concerns about corporate profits and household budgets. Higher inflation readings such as Thursday's report have also driven up U.S. bond yields and rates on loans benchmarked to those yields.
Interest rates on the average U.S. 30-year fixed mortgages topped 7% for the first time in more than a year, according to calculations from Mortgage News Daily.

Shares of the home builders retreated after weak housing data showed the toll that rising mortgage rates are taking. Used-home sales fell 2% in July to an annualized rate of 3.98 million. Lennar shares fell 3.5% at $77.90.
Shares of Macy's slid 4.7% to $20.50 even after the department store chain raised its sales growth projection for a second time this year after recording growth across its brands.
Designer Brands, owner of shoe store DSW, raised its full-year sales outlook, citing a strong start to the current quarter.

Apple shares rose 3.6% to $326.57 after analyst Gene Munster, a co-founder of Deepwater Asset Management, said design merits of the new foldable iPhone Duo could generate higher-than-anticipated demand for the device. Shares of Apple supplier Skyworks rose 10% to $84.03.
